newsitem.title: UK: FORECAST - UK producer prices to rise slightly.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST - UK producer prices to rise slightly.

text.p: Costs of raw materials for British factories are expected to pick up slightly in March after February's marked slowdown, but a small rise would still leave an encouraging picture for inflation, economists say.
"We're looking for not such a good month as February, but the government will still be able to claim excellent historical performance," said Mark Hale, economist at Sakura Finance.

Producer prices data, due for release at 0830 GMT on Monday, are forecast to show input prices rose a seasonally-adjusted 0.2 percent on the month, a small correction after February's figures which showed a 0.9 percent fall.
But input prices will still be much lower than March 1996 -- 6.5 percent down year-on-year compared with a year-on-year rate of -6.6 percent in February.
Output prices are forecast to rise around 0.1 percent in March for a year-on-year rate of 1.2 percent.
HSBC economist Jonathan Loynes said heavy downward pressure on input prices from the pound's eight month rally could have eased off after sterling's rise came to a halt last month.
Sterling's trade-weighted index averaged 97.4 in March -- the same level as February.
The dramatic fall in oil prices, which was also holding input prices down, also slowed last month.

"Ideally we'd love to see another fall in input prices given the fact oil prices fell off in February and sterling has been strong, but we feel the bulk of that news is already evident in the February numbers, and increases in other commodity prices could have overwhelmed the strength of the pound," said Hale.
But he added: "A rise of 0.2 percent wouldn't be terribly alarming, it would just bring us a bit closer to reality."

Analysts said even if producer prices did come out weaker than expected, that would not take the pressure off the government to raise interest rates to allow it a fighting chance of meeting its inflation target of 2.5 percent or less.
Hale said strong growth in other areas of the economy such as the strong services sector and high consumer confidence would keep the pressure on for an interest rate rise after the May 1 election.

"Manufacturing only represents about a fifth of the economy and it's the other four-fifths that we're really worried about," he said, adding that UK retail prices data on April 16 would be of key importance as an indicator of inflationary pressure.
Economists forecast the underlying inflation rate to fall to 2.8 percent for March from 2.9 in February.

After being left unchanged at Thursday's monetary meeting, interest rates are widely expected to rise from the current 6.0 percent level after the election, when opinion polls suggest opposition Labour's finance spokesman Gordon Brown to replace Chancellor Kenneth Clarke.

Mark Miller, UK economist at Morgan Stanley, said he saw the 6.0 percent interest rate increasing by 50 basis points after the May 7 monetary meeting, with the base rates reaching 7-1/4 percent by the end of 1997 and 8-1/4 percent by the end of 1998.

Hale said the PPI release was likely to give a small boost to the gilt market. "I doubt anything other than a shockingly large leap in the PPI figures on Monday will have a very large effect on sentiment," said Hale.
